Three ways of turning heart rate into training load. All three need your maximum and resting heart rate and grow with both duration and intensity.

# Stress score
Banister's TRIMP scaled so that one hour at your threshold heart rate scores 100, which makes it comparable with the stress scores of other apps.

# Banister TRIMP
Minutes weighted by the share of your heart rate reserve you used, rising exponentially the way blood lactate does.

# Edwards TRIMP
Minutes in five bands of maximum heart rate, from 50–60 % up to 90–100 %, weighted 1 to 5.

# Limits
Heart rate reacts little to strength training, so lifting sessions score lower than they feel.
No GPS: the watch records none in interval mode.

Your watch does not mark reps, so PacingLab finds them in the speed it records every second.

# How reps are found
- Stretches clearly faster than those around them are reps; the slower stretches in between are recoveries.
- Stretches shorter than 10 seconds are ignored.
- A run recorded just before or after the interval workout counts as warm-up or cool-down.

# The numbers
- Running and Recovery add up all reps and all recoveries.
- Distances come from the speed, scaled so that they add up to the distance the watch reported.
- Average heart rate is weighted by time; the maximum ignores single-sample spikes.

# Heart rate recovery
On recovery rows, the drop in heart rate from the rep's peak to one minute later (or to the end of a shorter recovery). It shows how quickly your body switches back to rest. Within a session, a smaller drop than after the earlier reps is a sign of fatigue; across sessions, a larger drop after the same work points to better fitness (Daanen 2012). Wrist sensors lag, so the peak is looked for up to 10 seconds after the rep ends.
Recovery rows: heart rate drop in the first minute.

Time, pace and average heart rate of each kilometre. The bar shows speed, from zero, against the fastest kilometre.\n\nDistance comes from the GPS track, or from the speed the watch records when there is no track, scaled to the distance the watch reported so that the splits add up the way it shows them. A last part shorter than 100 m is left out.

PacingLab finds sprints in the speed your watch records every second: bursts of at least 3 seconds faster than 18 km/h, with rest between them.

# The numbers
- Time and distance include the acceleration, from the moment you ran faster than a jog until you slowed down again.
- Top speed is the fastest three seconds of each sprint.
- Rest is the time until the next sprint.

# Limits
- Without GPS the watch estimates speed from your steps, which tends to read high at sprint speed. Compare sprints with each other rather than with a stopwatch.
- Heart rate barely reacts to a 10-second effort, which is why the time in zones of a sprint session looks easy.
Heart rate over the session, coloured by zone

Heart rate over the session and the time spent in each zone, using the heart rate values in force on the day of the session.

# The chart
- The line takes the colour of the zone it is in; dotted lines mark the zone boundaries, with their heart rate on the right.
- Touch the chart to read the time and heart rate.
- Gaps are pauses between recorded parts or moments without heart rate.

# 5 zones
Joe Friel's running zones, as a share of threshold heart rate (LTHR):
- Z1 Recovery: below 85 %
- Z2 Aerobic: 85–89 %
- Z3 Tempo: 90–94 %
- Z4 Threshold: 95–102 %
- Z5 VO2max: 103 % and above

# 3 zones
The polarized view used in endurance research:
- Below VT1: under 90 % of LTHR
- VT1 to VT2: 90 % of LTHR up to LTHR
- Above VT2: LTHR and above
Without a lab test, both thresholds are approximations.

# How time is counted
- Each heart rate sample counts until the next one, at most 15 seconds, so gaps in the recording do not inflate a zone.
- Wrist heart rate lags at the start of hard reps, so short reps show less time in the top zones than they deserve. Sprints of 10 seconds barely move heart rate at all; judge them by speed.
Set your maximum heart rate to see time in each zone.
